How Long Does It Take to Build a Website in 2026?

A realistic breakdown of website build timelines in 2026. From DIY builders to custom agency builds — see exactly how long each approach takes and what slows projects down.

If you are planning a new website, the first question is usually about cost. The second question is almost always about time. How long does it take to build a website? The honest answer: anywhere from a few hours to over a year. The real answer depends on what you are building, how you are building it, and how prepared you are when the project starts.

This guide breaks down realistic timelines for every type of website build in 2026. We cover DIY builders, template-based sites, custom agency builds, and enterprise platforms. We also walk through each phase of the process, identify the most common causes of delay, and show you how to keep your project on schedule.

Timeline by Build Method: The Honest Breakdown

The method you choose to build your website is the single biggest factor in how long it takes. Each approach has a different timeline, trade-off, and outcome. Here is what you can realistically expect.

Build Method Timeline Best For
DIY Website Builder
(Wix, Squarespace, Namecheap)		 1–3 days Hobby projects, personal sites, testing ideas
Template + Freelancer 2–4 weeks Small businesses on a tight budget
Custom Agency Build 4–8 weeks Businesses that need leads and growth
E-Commerce Website 8–16 weeks Online stores with products, payments, shipping
Enterprise Platform 3–6 months+ Large companies, custom integrations, SaaS

These ranges assume a typical project with standard complexity. A simple brochure site will land on the shorter end. A site with custom functionality, third-party integrations, or complex user flows will land on the longer end. The key is to match your timeline expectations to your build method from the start.

DIY Website Builders: Hours to Days

Platforms like Wix, Squarespace, and Namecheap Site Maker allow you to launch a basic website in a matter of hours. You pick a template, swap in your content, and publish. For a one-page landing site or a simple personal portfolio, this can be done in a single afternoon.

The trade-off is flexibility. You are limited to the platform's templates and features. Custom design is nearly impossible. SEO control is restricted. And if you ever want to move your site elsewhere, you are often locked in. For businesses that need to generate leads or revenue, DIY builders are usually a temporary solution at best.

Template + Freelancer: Weeks, Not Months

Hiring a freelancer to customize a pre-built template is a popular middle-ground option. A freelancer can set up a WordPress site with a premium theme, configure plugins, and tailor the design to your brand. This approach typically takes 2–4 weeks.

The risk here is quality and consistency. Not all freelancers follow the same process. Some skip discovery entirely and start building immediately, which leads to mismatched expectations and revision loops. Others rely heavily on page builder plugins that slow down your site and create maintenance headaches later. If you go this route, vet the freelancer's process carefully.

Custom Agency Build: The Professional Standard

A custom agency build is the gold standard for businesses that treat their website as a growth tool. At OnwardCraft, our custom builds typically take 4–8 weeks from kickoff to launch. This includes discovery, design, development, content, testing, and deployment.

The extra time is not wasted. It is invested in strategy, user experience, and conversion optimization. A custom site is built specifically for your audience, your goals, and your brand. It loads faster, ranks better, and converts at a higher rate than template-based alternatives. For most established small businesses, this is the right balance of speed and quality.

E-Commerce and Complex Builds: Months of Work

E-commerce websites, membership platforms, and sites with heavy custom functionality require significantly more time. Product catalogs, payment processing, user accounts, inventory management, and shipping integrations all add layers of complexity.

A typical e-commerce build takes 8–16 weeks. Enterprise platforms with custom backends, API integrations, or multi-user workflows can take 3–6 months or longer. These projects require detailed technical planning, extensive testing, and often multiple development sprints.

Phase-by-Phase: What Actually Happens and How Long Each Step Takes

Understanding the phases of a website build helps you set realistic expectations and avoid the surprises that derail timelines. Here is how a professional agency breaks down the work.

Phase 1: Discovery and Strategy (1–2 Weeks)

Discovery is the foundation of every successful website project. During this phase, the agency learns about your business, your audience, your competitors, and your goals. We define the sitemap, identify key pages, and establish the technical requirements.

This phase often takes longer than clients expect, and that is a good thing. Rushing discovery leads to scope changes later, which are far more expensive. A thorough discovery process prevents misalignment and sets the project up for smooth execution. At OnwardCraft, our discovery process is built to surface the insights that drive better design decisions.

Phase 2: Content Preparation (1–3 Weeks)

Content is the single biggest bottleneck in website projects. Copywriting, photography, and asset gathering always take longer than anticipated. If you are writing your own copy, expect this to add significant time to your project.

The best way to avoid delays is to start content early. Begin drafting copy during the discovery phase. Gather brand assets, logos, and photos before design starts. If you need professional copywriting or photography, budget extra time and cost for those deliverables. A site cannot launch without content, so this phase is non-negotiable.

Phase 3: Design (2–3 Weeks)

Design begins with wireframes — low-fidelity layouts that map out page structure and user flow. Once wireframes are approved, the visual design phase begins. This includes color schemes, typography, imagery, and interactive elements. Every page is designed for desktop, tablet, and mobile.

Revision rounds are built into this phase. Most agencies include 2–3 rounds of revisions. The key to staying on schedule is consolidated feedback. Designate one internal decision-maker, gather all stakeholder input, and deliver it in a single batch. Scattered feedback and "design by committee" are two of the fastest ways to extend your timeline.

Phase 4: Development (3–6 Weeks)

Development is where the design comes to life. The development team builds the site on your chosen platform, implements responsive layouts, configures CMS functionality, and sets up any integrations. This is also when SEO foundations are laid — meta tags, structured data, page speed optimization, and clean code.

Development time varies based on complexity. A simple brochure site might take 2–3 weeks. A site with custom animations, interactive features, or third-party integrations can take 4–6 weeks or more. The development phase is also when any custom functionality — booking systems, calculators, membership areas — is built and tested.

Phase 5: Testing and Quality Assurance (1–2 Weeks)

Testing is not an afterthought. It is a critical phase that ensures your site works correctly across devices, browsers, and screen sizes. The QA process includes:

  • Cross-browser testing (Chrome, Safari, Firefox, Edge)
  • Cross-device testing (desktop, tablet, mobile)
  • Form functionality and email delivery verification
  • Link checking and broken link fixes
  • Page speed and performance optimization
  • SEO meta tags and structured data validation
  • Accessibility compliance checks
  • Security and SSL configuration

Skipping or rushing QA leads to a broken launch. Forms that do not submit, pages that break on mobile, and slow load times all damage your credibility and conversion rates. A proper QA phase takes 1–2 weeks and is worth every day.

Phase 6: Launch and Post-Launch (2–3 Days)

Launch day involves connecting the domain, configuring DNS, enabling SSL, and performing final live testing. The site is pushed to production, search engines are notified, and analytics are verified.

Post-launch, most agencies provide a short support window to catch any issues that surface in the live environment. This is also when you should begin monitoring performance, tracking conversions, and planning ongoing improvements. A website is never truly "done" — it is a living asset that should evolve with your business.

The Biggest Causes of Delay (And How to Avoid Them)

Most website projects do not fail because of technical problems. They fail because of process problems. Here are the most common causes of delay and how to prevent them.

1. Late Content Delivery

This is the number one reason website timelines slip. Clients often underestimate how long it takes to write copy, gather photos, and prepare assets. When content is not ready by the development phase, the project stalls.

Solution: Start writing copy during discovery. Set a hard deadline for content delivery before design begins. If you cannot produce content internally, hire a copywriter early in the process.

2. Slow Feedback and Decision-Making

Every day you delay feedback adds days to the timeline. Design and development are sequential processes. If a designer is waiting a week for approval on wireframes, the entire project shifts back by a week.

Solution: Designate one decision-maker. Set a 48-hour feedback SLA. Consolidate all internal input before sending it to the agency.

3. Scope Changes Mid-Project

Adding a new page, changing the navigation structure, or requesting new features after development has started forces the team to backtrack. This is the most expensive type of delay.

Solution: Lock the scope during discovery. If new ideas emerge, add them to a "phase two" list instead of changing the current build.

4. Too Many Stakeholders

When five people need to approve every design decision, consensus becomes impossible. "Design by committee" produces bland, ineffective work and extends timelines indefinitely.

Solution: Limit the feedback circle to 2–3 people maximum. One person should have final approval authority.

5. Unprepared Brand Assets

If you do not have a logo, brand colors, or a style guide when design starts, the designer has to create those from scratch or work with incomplete information. This extends the design phase and often leads to rework.

Solution: Gather all brand assets before the project kickoff. If you need a rebrand, complete it before starting the website project.

Can AI Speed Up Website Builds in 2026?

Artificial intelligence has changed the website development landscape, but not in the way many people expect. AI tools can accelerate certain tasks — generating copy drafts, producing image assets, and automating code patterns — but they do not replace the strategic thinking and creative judgment that produce high-converting websites.

Here is where AI helps and where it falls short:

  • AI helps with: Drafting copy, generating image variations, automating repetitive code, suggesting SEO improvements, and speeding up early design iteration.
  • AI cannot replace: Strategic discovery, brand positioning, user experience design, conversion optimization, and quality assurance testing.

At OnwardCraft, we use AI as a tool to enhance our process, not replace it. It helps us move faster in the early stages, but the final product still requires human expertise in design, strategy, and development. A disciplined process with AI assistance will almost always outperform a rushed build that relies on AI alone.

DIY vs Hiring an Agency: The Timeline Trade-Off

One of the most common questions we hear is whether to build a website yourself or hire professionals. The timeline difference is dramatic, but so is the outcome difference.

DIY builders can get you online in days. But the result is a generic site that looks like thousands of others, converts poorly, and limits your growth. You will also spend 20–40 hours of your own time learning the platform, troubleshooting issues, and making design decisions without strategic guidance.

Hiring an agency takes longer — typically 4–8 weeks — but the result is a custom-built asset designed specifically for your business. You get strategic guidance, professional design, clean code, and ongoing support. Most importantly, you get a site that actually generates leads and revenue.

Frequently Asked Questions

How long does it take to build a simple 5-page website?

A simple 5-page brochure website takes 3–5 weeks with a professional agency. This includes discovery, design, development, and testing. With a freelancer using a template, it can take 2–4 weeks. With a DIY builder, it can be done in 1–3 days, though the quality and customization will be limited.

How long does it take to build an e-commerce website?

An e-commerce website typically takes 8–16 weeks. The timeline depends on the number of products, payment integrations, shipping configurations, and any custom features. A small store with 10–20 products on Shopify can be launched in 4–6 weeks. A custom-built e-commerce platform with hundreds of products and complex functionality can take 3–6 months.

What is the fastest way to build a website?

The fastest way is a DIY website builder like Wix or Squarespace. You can launch a basic site in a few hours. However, speed comes at the cost of customization, performance, and conversion potential. For businesses that need to generate revenue, a professional build is faster in the long run because it does not require a rebuild 6–12 months later.

Can a website be built in one week?

Technically, yes — if you use a template or DIY builder and have all content ready. However, a one-week build skips discovery, strategy, and quality assurance. The result is usually a site that looks rushed, performs poorly, and fails to convert. For any business that depends on its website for leads or sales, one week is not enough.

What slows down a website project the most?

Late content delivery is the single biggest cause of delays. Other major factors include slow client feedback, scope changes mid-project, too many stakeholders, and unprepared brand assets. The good news is that all of these are preventable with proper planning and clear communication.

How can I speed up my website build?

Prepare your content before the project starts. Designate one decision-maker for feedback. Lock the project scope during discovery. Gather all brand assets upfront. Respond to feedback requests within 48 hours. And choose an agency with a proven process — like ours at OnwardCraft — that is designed to keep projects on track.

The timeline for building a website in 2026 ranges from a few hours to several months. The right timeline for your project depends on your goals, your budget, and how you want your site to perform. A rushed build might get you online faster, but a disciplined, professional build will get you results that last. If you are ready to build a website that drives real business growth, let us talk.
